@stjbs.bsky.social and Ko Lyn Cheang interviewed 12 people with serious conditions in detention and documented eight cases where independent physicians said the delays could have caused life-threatening harm. One had lived here 52 years and waited months for an oncologist.

ICE's 2025 detention standards require medical care at no cost to the detainee. People are getting bills anyway. One man was pursued by debt collectors over a $634 blood test. Another was handed $17,210 after emergency gallbladder surgery he had while handcuffed.

Six providers were waiting on nearly $5.6 million as of July. Scripps Health in San Diego is owed $3 million. A nonprofit ambulance service in rural Pennsylvania is owed about $197,000, or 13 percent of its annual revenue, and has kept answering the calls.

The cause is administrative. The VA ended its arrangement to process ICE's medical claims from outside specialists last October. ICE called the result an "absolute emergency" in writing and issued an internal directive limiting offsite care and medication.

ICE has not paid a medical provider for detainee care since October 3, 2025. Hospitals and ambulance services are owed millions, and detainees are billed for care ICE says must be free. New from @sfchronicle.com: www.sfchronicle.com/politics/art...

The morning of the conversation an attorney emailed about a client deported mid-crisis who died at home a week later, and asked whether the name could go on the dashboard. I had to say no. That death produces no notification and no report.

Two groups sit outside the count entirely. People who had the same medical emergency under the same conditions and survived by chance, and people released or deported who died afterward, harder to see since the 30-day post-release tracking requirement was rolled back.

There is money underneath this. Sheriffs across the U.S. South told me repeatedly that one heart attack or one diabetic seizure can blow through a jail's medical budget for the year, so there is a financial reason to release a medically fragile person rather than treat them.

Custody is broader than the inside of a facility, so we record both the last facility a person was held in and the place they actually died. A map counting only deaths inside facilities would show none of California's six under this administration.
